dedupe_keys.name: disaster debris management requirements challenges and federal agency roles congressional research service r44941 2017

description: This Congressional Research Service report explains how disaster debris is managed in the United States and who is responsible for it. After hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, tornadoes, wildfires or winter storms, debris can include soil and sediment, trees and vegetation, household garbage and belongings, construction and demolition waste up to whole houses, vehicles, spoiled food, refrigerators and other white goods, and household hazardous waste, any of which may be contaminated. The report sets out the federal and state waste rules that still apply after a disaster and the main challenges: sheer volume, separating contaminated wastes, and uneven participation by returning residents. It then describes the roles of FEMA, which funds debris removal after major disaster declarations, the US Army Corps of Engineers, which can clear rights of way, collect curbside waste and demolish property, and EPA, which helps with contaminated debris and household hazardous waste, and of state and local governments. The 16-page report is free to download as a PDF from congress.gov. Coverage is US federal policy as of September 2017. Caveats: a policy overview without quantities, and it has not been updated since 2017. Simulation uses: debris categories, agency responsibilities and constraints for disaster waste and recovery models. Related records: OpenFEMA (data-openfema) holds the Public Assistance project data that record debris removal spending, and the Venezuela 2026 earthquake debris assessment (data-venezuela-2026-earthquake-debris-assessment) is an example of debris quantities after a single event.
